1:
Robertson notes that this is the first time the two parties appear in combination, and makes the alliance the point: they disliked each other exceedingly, but hated Jesus more than they hated each other, and their hostility had grown rather than cooled during his absence. Origen presses the same oddity harder, since the disagreement between them ran to the most essential truths — the Pharisees championing the resurrection of the dead and hoping for a world to come, the Sadducees knowing of nothing in store for a man after this life, whether he has been advancing towards virtue or has made no effort at all to come out from the mountains of wickedness — and yet these agree in order to tempt him, as Herod and Pilate became friends with one another in order to kill him. Henry says the same from the other end: men at variance among themselves were unanimous in opposing Christ, because his doctrine equally overthrew the Sadducees’ denial of spirits and a future state and the Pharisees’ pride, tyranny and hypocrisy.

Gill locates the deputation, not from Jerusalem this time but from the neighbouring places, Galilean Sadducees and Pharisees of the sort the Mishnah mentions. Ellicott finds the presence of the second sect genuinely noticeable, since they appear nowhere else in the Galilean ministry, and explains it from Mark’s wording of the warning a few verses later, where the leaven of Herod stands where Matthew has the leaven of the Sadducees: the Herodians were the Galilean Sadducees, so the union of two hostile parties here continues an alliance that had begun after the protest about false reverence for the Sabbath.

What sign was actually wanted is answered most concretely by Remigius, who finds it in John: after the feeding of the five thousand the crowd asked what sign he did, and said that their fathers ate manna in the desert, bread given them from heaven; so the demand here means, cause it to rain manna for a day or two, that the whole people may eat as they did in the wilderness. Barnes keeps it general — some miraculous appearance in the sky, such as the prophets had given, Samuel causing it to thunder and Isaiah turning back the shadow — on the assumption that a Messiah’s miracles would not all be confined to the earth. Wesley suggests a test behind the choice, that such a sign they imagined Satan could not counterfeit. Robertson doubts they had any definite idea at all beyond embarrassing him, noting only that the Jewish apocalypses did speak of spectacular displays of power by the Son of Man.

Remigius calls the request a wondrous blindness, since they asked for a sign from heaven as though what they were already looking at were not signs. Calvin conjectures from Mark that this was a last resource after they had been beaten in argument, obstinate men being accustomed, when reduced to extremities, to introduce something foreign to the subject rather than yield to the truth; he guesses the dispute had been about Christ’s calling, why he ventured any innovation and made such lofty pretensions, and he is certain that a hundred signs would have weighed no more with them than the testimonies of Scripture already had. Hilary reads the departure at the end of the exchange as a verdict: we do not read here, as we do elsewhere, that he sent the multitudes away and departed, but that he left these men, because the error of unbelief held the minds of the presumptuous.
2:
Barnes paraphrases the answer as an argument from their own habits: you have indications by which you judge the weather, and evidence in the redness of the sky, so there are indications enough on which to judge of me and of these times — the miracles, and the state of affairs in Judea. He adds that almost all nations have read a red sky the same way. Robertson glosses the word for fair weather as an old poetic compound formed on the name of the ruler of the air and giver of good weather, which turns up on the Rosetta Stone and in a fourth-century papyrus for the calm that made it impossible to sail a boat; and he remarks that men still say the sky is red at sunset. Calvin calls the comparison beautiful and highly appropriate: the aspect of the sky is changeable, so that a storm sometimes rises unexpectedly and fair weather springs up where none was looked for, and yet the instructions of nature are enough to let a man predict the day — which is why he asks how the kingdom of God goes unrecognised when it is made known by signs not less plain.

The verses are a textual problem, and three of them say so. Ellicott reports that some of the best manuscripts, the Vatican and Sinaitic among them, omit the whole of these words; he cannot think them interpolated by a later transcriber, given their singular originality of form, and so has to account for the omission instead — they are absent from Mark, which of itself shows that reports of the answer circulated without them, and a transcriber may have been unable to read their meaning, or may have wished to bring the two Gospels into closer agreement. Robertson gives the same evidence, notes that another witness drops part of the verse, observes the close resemblance to a passage in Luke, and records that McNeile rejects the words here while Westcott and Hort bracket them; his own answer is that Jesus often repeated his sayings, though he passes on Zahn’s suggestion that Papias added them to Matthew. Jerome had met the difficulty long before, reporting that it is not found in most copies of the Greek text while holding the sense clear enough, that fair and rainy days may be foretold from the condition and harmony of the elements.

Calvin and Clarke both turn the comparison into an indictment. Calvin says the words remind them that his power had been manifested sufficiently, so that they must have recognised the day of their visitation had they not of their own accord shut their eyes and refused the clearest light. Clarke presses the same point to its consequence: the signs of fair and foul weather they are in the constant habit of observing do not fail them, and the doctrine preached and the miracles worked among them are signs just as sure that the day-spring from on high has visited them for their salvation — but if they refuse to hear and continue in darkness, the red and gloomy cloud of vindictive justice will pour out a storm of wrath that sweeps them from the face of the earth.
3:
Clarke observes that these signs were watched in much the same way among the Romans and most other peoples, and quotes the lines from the Georgics in which the colour of the setting sun portends high winds and furious tempests, livid blue bodes wet weather, and dusky spots streaked with red declare wind, rain, storms and elemental war together. Robertson glosses the word for lowring as a sky covered with cloud, a word used also of a gloomy countenance — of the rich young ruler in Mark — and found nowhere else in the New Testament, and notes that the word for foul weather is the ordinary one for winter and a storm; he adds that this very sign of a rainy day is still in use. Gill describes the daily habit plainly, rising in the morning and taking a survey of the heavens.

Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic instance of the same curiosity about the seasons of the heavens and the temper of the air. At the going out of the last day of the feast of Tabernacles everyone watched the rising of the smoke: if it bent northward the poor rejoiced and the rich were troubled, because there would be much rain in the following year and the fruits would be corrupted; if southward the poor grieved and the rich rejoiced, for there would be fewer rains and the fruit would be sound; if eastward all rejoiced, and if westward all were troubled.

Calvin explains the name the questioners are given. They are called hypocrites because they pretend to ask for something which, if it were exhibited to them, they are resolved not to observe; and the reproof applies nearly to the whole world, since men direct their ingenuity and apply their senses to immediate advantage, so that scarcely a man is not tolerably well acquainted with the means of gaining his object. How then does it come about, Calvin asks, that we feel no concern about the signs by which God invites us to himself — unless every man gives himself up to willing indifference and extinguishes the light that is offered him. Robertson draws the opposite moral from the same clause, that it is not always easy to discriminate the signs of one’s own time, that men are numerous with patent keys to it all, and that we ought not to be blind when others are gullible. Wesley says only what the signs were: those which evidently show that this is the time of the Messiah.
4:
Robertson records that the words are the same as those used four chapters earlier, with only the title of the prophet added, and calls it a real doublet; Gill says the same thing without the term, that he says here what he had said to the Pharisees on a like occasion. Barnes brings in Mark’s detail that he sighed deeply in spirit, and reads feeling into it: the reply was not made without emotion, the speaker being greatly affected with their perverseness and obstinacy. Ellicott notes that Mark’s version of the refusal is the more absolute of the two, since there no sign at all shall be given to this generation — none, that is, of the kind being demanded.

Clarke explains the charge of adultery from the standing figure of the Scriptures, where the people are married to the Most High and, like a disloyal wife, forsake their true husband to unite themselves with Satan and sin. He reads the verb as seeking sign upon sign, still another sign, when the miracles already worked had demonstrated the divine mission and only one thing remained necessary — to take away the scandal of the cross and death, to fulfil the Scriptures and to establish the Christian religion — namely the resurrection, typified in the case of Jonah. Wesley compresses the whole diagnosis: they would seek no further sign did not their wickedness, their love of the world which is spiritual adultery, blind their understanding. Calvin draws a distinction the others pass over: they are not condemned merely for demanding a sign, since the Lord sometimes permitted his people to do that, but because they deliberately provoke God; and what is threatened is that after rising from the dead he will be a prophet like Jonah, which strictly means that the risen Christ would in every place cause the voice of his Gospel to be distinctly heard.

Origen answers the demand on its own terms, which the rest leave alone. The sign of Jonah was not merely a sign but a sign from heaven, measured by the very question asked; so that even to men who were tempting him and asking for a heavenly sign he nevertheless gave one, out of his own great goodness. The three days and nights in the whale’s belly are the point of comparison, and the resurrection they figure came from heaven, which is exactly what the questioners had stipulated for and did not recognise when it was promised them.
5:
Barnes and Clarke fix the crossing: the exchange with the Pharisees had taken place on the east of the sea of Galilee, and they crossed again to the west, Clarke naming the coast of Bethsaida on a journey that was heading for Caesarea. Ellicott prefers the plain past, that they forgot, and brings in Mark’s precision that they had but one loaf with them; he offers two explanations, either that the suddenness of their Lord’s departure robbed them of their customary forethought, or that they were beginning to depend wrongly on the wonder-working power, as though it would be used to render forethought needless for themselves rather than to supply the wants of a famished multitude. Robertson guesses at the hurry to leave Galilee, probably in the same boat they had come across in. Gill places the moment of recollection either in the ship or on the way up from the shore.

Two of the fathers will not have the lapse counted against them. Henry hopes their minds and memories were filled with better things, and remarks that Christ’s disciples are often men with no great forecast for the world. Remigius makes it a positive virtue: they were bound to their Master with so great affection that they were unwilling to part from him for even a moment of time, and it is worth observing how far they were from any longing for delicacies when they took so little care for necessaries that they forgot the bread without which human weakness cannot support itself.

Origen reads the forgetting as a figure of the crossing itself. The loaves they had before they came to the other side were no longer useful to them once they had crossed, since they needed one kind of loaf before and a different kind after; and being careless about loaves on the way over, they left them behind. Those who arrived on the other side were disciples who had passed from things material to things spiritual, and from things sensible to those which are intellectual.

Chrysostom presses the question why the warning took the form it did, rather than saying plainly, take heed of the doctrine of the Pharisees. Because he meant to remind them at the same time of what had been done in the multiplication of the loaves, knowing them to be forgetful: a charge delivered bluntly and unprompted would have seemed unreasonable, where finding fault on an occasion they had furnished themselves prepared the way for it. The Gloss ties the warning to the departure just recorded, that as the Lord had left the Pharisees on account of their unbelief he now teaches his disciples to be on their guard against their doctrine. Calvin sets out how crowded the danger was: the Pharisees had come, the Sadducees joined them, and apart from both stood Herod, a very wicked man and a corrupter of sound doctrine; among such hazards the warning was necessary, since the human mind has a natural inclination towards vanity and errors, and when a man is surrounded by wicked inventions and spurious doctrines nothing is easier than to drift away.
6:
Barnes explains the figure by how leaven actually behaves: it passes through the flour and sets it fermenting, secretly and silently but certainly, so that nobody sees its progress. The doctrines in question were of the same kind, insinuating, artful and plausible, concealing their real tendency, instilled quietly into the mind and then pervading every faculty. Clarke puts it as a rule about creeds: bad doctrines act in the soul as leaven does in meal, assimilating the whole spirit to their own nature, and a man’s particular creed has a greater influence on his temper and conduct than most people are aware of — the pride, hypocrisy and worldly-mindedness which made up this leaven ruining the greater part of the world. Wesley calls the figure elegant for the same reason, that false doctrine spreads in the soul, or in the Church, as leaven spreads in meal.

Lightfoot explains why the disciples took the word literally, and gives two reasons. They had seldom heard leaven used of doctrine: the metaphorical use was common enough among them in a bad sense, for evil affections and the naughtiness of the heart — he quotes a prayer that the Lord of ages would subdue the leaven which is in the lump — but for false teaching it was rare if it occurred at all. Barnes reaches the same conclusion independently, that no other instance of the usage is to be found among the Jews, which is why the hearers reasoned about bread.

Jerome turns the warning into a positive instruction and then widens it. Whoever takes heed of this leaven does not observe the precepts of the Law and of the letter, and neglects the traditions of men that he may do the commandments of God; and this is the leaven the Apostle means when he says that a little leaven leavens the whole lump. By every means, Jerome adds, the leaven of Marcion and Valentinus and all the heretics is to be avoided, for the nature of leaven is such that when mixed with flour what seemed a little increases to a great quantity and brings the whole mixture to its own flavour — so a heretical doctrine which has cast only a small spark into the breast raises a mighty flame in a short time. Hilary gives the admonition a different direction: the Apostles are warned not to be partakers in the doctrine of the Jews, since the works of the Law were established to produce faith and to prefigure what was to follow, and men on whose own times the truth itself had come should look for no further types of it.

Ellicott notes that Mark reports the saying differently, pairing the leaven of the Pharisees with the leaven of Herod; and if a choice has to be made he would take that as the form actually spoken, this Evangelist or the report he followed substituting the better-known Sadducees for the less familiar Herodians. He thinks the form of the warning was determined by what had just happened, the Master seeing the perplexed looks and hearing the self-reproaching or mutually accusing whispers and making them the text of a proverb which is a concentrated parable.
7:
Robertson calls the scene pathetic, the almost jejune inability of the disciples to take a parabolic warning after the collision with both parties that had happened only moments before; the imperfect tense means they kept the discussion up, and the word is loaves rather than bread. Clarke, following Lightfoot, repeats that the term for leaven was rarely used among the Jews of doctrine, so the meaning did not immediately reach them — and then turns the failure into a complaint about the human mind in general, which perceives bodily wants with the utmost readiness and seeks a supply with all speed, while the necessities of the soul are rarely discovered at all, though they press harder and their supply matters infinitely more. Gill allows two accounts of the perplexity: either they could not see what the caution meant and why it was given, or they were anxiously concerned about where provisions were to come from.

Ellicott hears something else in the self-questioning. There is a childish naivete in it which testifies to the absolute originality and truthfulness of the record, and so to the genuineness of the question that follows, since that question assumes the reality of the two earlier miracles. The train of thought connecting the warning with the missing bread was probably hardly formulated even in their own minds; and it may be that they imagined that as a Pharisee would not eat bread defiled by the touch of a heathen or a publican, so their Master was forbidding them, however great their need, to take food at the hands of either.

Origen reads the rebuke as falling on thought alone, and draws a general rule from it. We are sometimes convicted and reproached as being of little faith in respect only of the reasonings we reason within ourselves; and just as a man commits adultery in his heart without proceeding to the overt act, so he commits in his heart the rest of the things that are forbidden. As the first will be punished proportionately to adultery of that kind, so also will the man who has stolen in his heart only, which is what makes an unspoken anxiety about loaves worth a reproof at all.
8:
Gill makes the point that nothing was overheard: the debates were known by omniscience, the doubts and unbelief and anxious solicitude of their minds along with their private reasonings. Clarke adds a textual note, that the pronoun after the verb is wanting in a long list of manuscripts and in the Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic and Vulgate, besides two of the Greek fathers, that Mill approves the omission and Griesbach has left it out of the text.

Ellicott is careful about what is being reproved. It is not the want of discernment that made them slow to take the similitude, since discernment depends in part on imaginative power or acquired culture and they were not responsible for lacking either; it is the want of faith. Their memory of how their wants had twice been supplied might at least have taught them that no such extreme necessity as they were picturing was likely to arise while he was with them, and therefore that their gross carnal reading of his words could not possibly be the right one. Clarke softens the epithet: there are degrees in faith as in the other graces of the Spirit, and a little faith may be the seed of great faith and is not to be despised, though many who ought to be strong have only a small measure of it. Wesley turns the question into its own answer — why be troubled about this, when a word would supply them if need required.

Chrysostom asks why the rebuke comes now rather than earlier, since the question where so much bread was to be had in the wilderness looked the more fitting occasion. His answer is twofold: no blame was given then, lest he should seem to have been urged by it into working the miracle, and he was unwilling to find fault with them in front of the people; and there is more reason in the charge here, because after two multiplications of loaves they were still anxious about food. Calvin diagnoses the mistake itself. The warning is rashly taken as though Christ intended only to withdraw them from outward intercourse, since it was customary among the Jews not to eat in the company of irreligious men and the disciples supposed the Pharisees classed with such people. That ignorance might perhaps have been borne with, Calvin says, but they are forgetful of a favour lately received and do not consider that the remedy is in their Master’s own power. Robertson counts four pungent questions about intellectual dulness in the verses that follow, and remarks that every teacher recognises this strain upon the patience of the Teacher of teachers.
9:
Gill allows two things that might be meant by understanding here: either the sense of the advice just given, or, as he prefers, the almighty power displayed in the two feedings — five thousand at one time and four thousand at another out of a very small quantity of provision — since it is to those that the word points. Robertson observes that the two miracles are kept distinct even in the vocabulary, a different word being used for the baskets of the five thousand from the word used of the four thousand, and the distinction holding in both accounts.

Clarke cannot get past the improbability of the lapse. How astonishing that these men should have any fear of lacking bread after seeing the two miracles alluded to. Men perceive their bodily wants quickly enough and are querulous until they are supplied, and then forget the mercy as quickly, so that God gets few returns of gratitude for his kindnesses; and to make men deeply sensible of his favours he is induced to let them often be in want.

Chrysostom notices the manner rather than the matter. Observe with what mildness the rebuke is given: he makes the excuse himself in the very question, asking whether they do not yet understand nor remember the five loaves, and by that calling to mind what was past while rousing their attention to what was to come. On his reading the question is not a demand for an answer but a prompt, supplying the memory it accuses them of lacking.

Henry makes the same observation about what is NOT rebuked. He does not chide them for their little forecast, as they expected he would; and Henry draws the domestic lesson, that parents and masters must not be angry at the forgetfulness of children and servants beyond what is needed to make them take more heed another time, since we are all apt to forget our duty, and that a fault may be excused as an oversight. See how easily the disciples’ carelessness was forgiven, he says, though it was in so material a point as taking bread.
10:
Gill supplies the plain sense: have you forgotten the other miracle, done only a very little while ago, when four thousand men besides women and children were fed with seven loaves and a few small fishes. Robertson adds that the second feeding keeps its own vocabulary, the word for these baskets differing from the word used of the earlier ones, so that the two reckonings are not run together and the question counts two distinct occasions rather than one remembered twice.

Chrysostom measures the effect of the reproof instead of its content. To learn what force it had upon the disciples, and how it roused their sluggish spirit, one has only to read what the Evangelist says a verse or two later; and the instruction drew them away from Jewish observances, made them attentive where they had been careless, and raised them out of their little faith, so that whenever their provision of bread seemed small they should have no fear about food but should despise all such things.

Origen identifies what the leaven was that made the warning necessary at the crossing. There was a certain lump of teaching and of truly ancient leaven, the teaching according to the bare letter, and on that account not freed from the things the letter carries with it; and perhaps it was to turn back those who, having crossed to the other side, had begun in the spirit, from running back to carnal things, that the charge to take heed and beware was given to them only once they were over.

Henry closes the episode with a distinction worth the two verses it takes. The weakness and shiftlessness of good people in their worldly affairs is what men are apt to condemn them for, but it is not so great an offence to Christ as their inordinate care and anxiety about those same things; so the mean has to be kept between the extremes of carelessness and carefulness. He adds that though the disciples may be brought into want and straits through their own want of thought, they are still encouraged to trust their Master for relief, and that this must not be turned into an excuse for refusing charity to the really poor on the ground that they should have managed better.
11:
Origen describes what the question does for men caught by an ambiguity. The disciples were distracted by the double sense of loaf and leaven, and are now told in an undisguised fashion that the subject was never sensible bread but the leaven in a teaching; and though the interpretation is still not laid bare and the language stays metaphorical, that much was enough for them to see that what the Saviour meant by leaven was what the Pharisees and Sadducees were teaching. Ellicott makes the reticence deliberate: true to his method of education he does not interpret the parable himself but is content to suggest the train of thought that leads to the interpretation, and the disciples, slow of heart as they were, followed the clue — memory at last quickened faith, and faith supplied the imaginative insight that sees its way through parables and dark sayings. Origen attaches a condition to the whole transaction: so long as we have Jesus with us, fulfilling the promise he made, the equivocal word can be cleared up for us as it was for them.

Gill paraphrases the exasperation without softening it: that you should be so senseless and void of thought, after such instances, as to imagine I concerned myself with what bread you brought along. Wesley supplies the elliptical sense of the opening words, that besides all this they do not understand that bread was never what the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees meant.

Clarke locates the fault and then names what was finally grasped. We are not deficient in spiritual knowledge because we have had no opportunity of acquainting ourselves with God, he says, but because we did not improve the advantages we had; and how deep and ruinous our ignorance would be if God did not give line upon line and precept upon precept, here a little and there a little. What they now perceived was a warning on two fronts: against the superstition of the Pharisees, which produced hypocrisy, pride and envy, and against the doctrine of the Sadducees, which denied the existence of a spiritual world, the immortality of the soul, the resurrection of the body and the providence of God.
12:
Gill notes that the understanding came without any further explication of the meaning; Robertson parses the aorist of a verb for grasping or comprehending and says they saw the point only after this elaborate rebuke, namely that by leaven teaching was meant. Barnes sets out five respects in which erroneous doctrines answer to the figure: they are slight and unimportant in appearance at first; they are insinuated into the soul unawares and silently, and are difficult to detect; they act gradually; they act most certainly; and they pervade the whole soul, bringing every faculty under their control.

Ellicott would render the noun as teaching rather than doctrine, meaning not so much the formulated dogmas of a sect as its general drift and tendency. The leaven of the one party is named expressly in Luke as hypocrisy — the unreality of a life respectable, rigid, outwardly religious, even earnest in its zeal, and yet wanting the humility and love which are of the essence of true holiness. That of the Sadducees and of Herod is nowhere specially defined, but Ellicott takes it for the more open form of worldliness and self-indulgence which allied itself with their denial of the resurrection and therefore of eternal life.

Calvin reads the word as a deliberate contrast. It stands against the pure and uncorrupted word of God; and although the same figure had been used favourably a few chapters earlier, where the Gospel itself resembles leaven, Scripture for the most part employs the word of some foreign substance by which the native purity of a thing is impaired. What is set against what here is the naked truth of God on one side and the inventions men contrive out of their own brain on the other; and Calvin will not allow the sophist to escape by pleading that this cannot be meant of every kind of doctrine. Barnes points the reference back a chapter, to the tradition of the elders and the washing of hands, as the specimen of the teaching the disciples had just been warned off; which makes the leaven something they had already watched working rather than an abstraction.
13:
The place is identified at length because there were two cities of the name. Barnes, Clarke and Gill distinguish it from the Caesarea on the Mediterranean: it had been Leshem, then Dan, then Paneas from the fountain of Jordan beside it, until Philip the tetrarch rebuilt it and named it for Tiberius Caesar, his own name added to keep the two apart. Jerome names the builder as Herod’s brother, tetrarch of Ituraea. Robertson places it on a spur of Mount Hermon, and Barnes reports it reduced in his own day to some two hundred houses. Ellicott reconstructs the route that led there — from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon to the eastern shore of the lake, by ship to Magdala and Dalmanutha, across again to the eastern Bethsaida, and so northward — and finds in it an obvious withdrawal from the populous cities which had rejected him.

Why the question was asked in that particular place is answered three ways. Chrysostom says he led his disciples far out of the way of the Jews so that, being set free from all fear, they might say freely what was in their mind. The Gloss ties it to the warning just given: having taken his disciples out of the teaching of the Pharisees, he lays the foundations of the Gospel doctrine deep, and the naming of the place gives the moment its solemnity; before confirming them he would first clear other men’s errors out of their minds. Henry makes the remoteness practical: in that far corner there was less flocking after him and so leisure for private conversation, from which he draws the rule that ministers abridged in their public work should do the more in their own families.

The form of the question is pressed as hard as its setting. Jerome calls it beautifully put: those who speak of the Son of Man are men, while those who understood his divine nature are called not men but gods, and the wording avoids asking ostentatiously about himself. He adds that wherever the Old Testament has Son of Man the Hebrew phrase is Son of Adam. Hilary takes the title to imply that something ought to be thought of him beyond what appeared, and denies that the question was a confession of himself, since what he asked after was concealed and the faith of believers ought to reach for it; from which he derives a rule, that the Son of God is not to be named without the Son of Man, one without the other offering no hope of salvation. Lightfoot adds that the title bespeaks the seed promised to Adam, the second Adam, and silently confutes a double Jewish ignorance about the Messiah’s origin.

On why he should ask at all, Raban denies any ignorance in it: he asks his disciples so as to reward their confession of a right faith, and asks after the opinions of those outside so that, the wrong ones being set out first, the disciples might be proved to have their confession not from common report but out of the hidden treasure of the Lord’s revelation. Chrysostom notices which group is canvassed — not the Scribes and Pharisees but men in general, whose minds were not perverted to evil: their opinion of Christ fell far below what it should have been yet was free from wilful wickedness, where the Pharisees’ was full of malice. Origen reads a method into it, that we should always investigate what opinion men form of us, cutting off occasions of ill and multiplying occasions of good. Robertson calls it an examination, the inchoative imperfect meaning that he began to question them. Cyril of Jerusalem gives the motive as instruction and not vain-glory: he wished to show them the truth, lest, dwelling with the Only-begotten of God, they should think lightly of him as of some mere man.
14:
Robertson says the disciples were ready to answer, knowing that popular opinion was divided, and that four distinct views are offered; he cannot resist the aside that it is always a risky thing for a pastor to ask people’s opinion of him. Gill traces the first of them: some of the Jews held that this was John the Baptist risen from the dead, a notion which spread through Herod’s court and which Herod himself came to accept. Barnes explains what made it plausible, the many miracles and the strong resemblance to John in manner of life and in the doctrines taught. Wesley accounts for the last of the four from a current tradition among the Jews, that either Jeremiah or some other of the ancient prophets would rise again before the Messiah came.

Ellicott values the verse for what it preserves. It is one of the very few passages indicating the impressions which had hardened into beliefs among the people about his character and mission; and each of them rests on a popular doctrine of transmigration to which the Pharisees had given a place in their teaching — the great actors of the past being still in existence and liable, at any great national crisis, to reappear in order to continue and complete their work.

Lightfoot asks why Jeremiah alone of all the prophets is named, and makes two observations about the shape of the expectation. Recourse is had here to the memory of the dead, from whom the Messiah should spring, rather than to the living, perhaps because the piety which had shone out in those deceased persons could not in those days be looked for in anyone alive; and they may have thought besides that the kingdom of the Messiah would arise only after the resurrection. He records that one of the Babylonian Gemarists suspected Daniel, raised from the dead, of being the Messiah.

Calvin is interested in whose errors these were. The inquiry does not touch the open enemies of Christ, nor ungodly scoffers, but the sounder and better part of the people, who might be called the choice and flower of the Church; only those are mentioned who spoke of Christ with respect, and yet, though they aimed at the truth, not one of them reaches it — all go astray in their own vain fancies. From which Calvin infers how great the weakness of the human mind is, since it is not only unable of itself to understand what is right or true, but coins errors even out of true principles.
15:
Both the grammarians fasten on the pronoun. Robertson says this is what matters and what Jesus wanted to hear, and notes its emphatic position. Ellicott finds it doubly emphasised in the Greek — but ye, whom say ye? — and hears the question as parallel in tone, though not in form, to the one put after the desertion at Capernaum: had they still a distinct faith of their own, or were they too falling back into these popular surmises?

Gill notices two things about the way the second question is framed. No further notice is taken of the different sentiments of men, and the question he had chiefly in view is put directly, to get their own sense of him; and it is put in a different form, the phrase about the Son of Man being left out, because they knew him to be more than a man and his mean appearance had never been an offence to them, since they had believed in him and become his followers. But believing, Gill adds, was not enough: they must confess him too, and both are necessary.

Calvin reads the division of the question as a division of the company. The disciples are distinguished from the rest of the crowd, to make it evident that whatever differences exist among other men we at least ought not to be led aside from the unity of faith; and those who honestly submit to Christ, without attempting to mix any inventions of their own brain with the Gospel, will never want the true light. The greatest vigilance is necessary all the same, so that though the whole world be carried away by its own inventions believers may continually adhere to Christ — and Calvin names the method used against them, that Satan, unable to rob the Jews of the conviction they had from the Law and the Prophets that Christ would come, changed him instead into various shapes.

Cyril of Jerusalem explains why the second question is put to this particular audience. The others may be excused for not knowing, he has Christ say, but you, my Apostles, who in my name cleanse lepers and cast out devils and raise the dead, ought not to be ignorant of him through whom you do these things. On that reading the change of pronoun is not a change of subject but a change of standard: the same ignorance which is pardonable in the crowd outside has become inexcusable in men who have been working miracles with his name in their mouths.
16:
Who was speaking, and for whom, is settled much the same way by all of them. Barnes has Peter expressing the views of the apostles with characteristic forwardness; Wesley says he was generally the most forward to speak. Gill allows either account, that he spoke of his own accord and for himself, being a warm and zealous man who dearly loved Christ and was ready to confess him, or that he spoke as the mouth of the rest, in their name and with their consent, or at least knowing full well the sentiments of their minds. Ellicott combines the two: the confession was made partly as the representative of the others and partly, as the promise which follows implies, out of the personal fervour of his character — he believed himself, and had impressed his faith upon them.

Clarke calls every word of it emphatic, a most concise and yet comprehensive confession: the title Christ points out the office, the Son designates the person, which is why the two are so frequently joined in the new covenant, and the last phrase is literally of God the Living One — a character applied to the Supreme Being not only to distinguish him from the dead idols of paganism but to mark him as the source of life; Clarke notes a manuscript which reads the Saviour in place of the Living One. Barnes adds that the term Son is used here by way of eminence, in a peculiar sense, an appellation understood as implying divinity, and that living distinguishes the true God from idols which are lifeless blocks and stones. Robertson counts the four Greek articles, calls it a noble confession but not a new claim, since Peter had said as much when the multitude deserted at Capernaum, and observes that the word Messiah had been avoided since the early ministry because of its political meaning to the people, where now it is used plainly.

Ellicott sets the three reports side by side — Mark giving simply that thou art the Christ, Luke the Christ of God — and judges the variations interesting for the question of literal inspiration without their affecting the meaning, the fullest of the three being receivable without hesitation as the most authentic. Calvin measures the confession by what it contains: short as it is, it embraces the whole of our salvation, since the designation takes in both an everlasting Kingdom and an everlasting Priesthood — to reconcile us to God, to obtain a perfect righteousness by expiating our sins through his sacrifice, and, having received us under his protection, to uphold and enrich us with every kind of blessing. He notes that the title had anciently belonged to kings anointed by divine command.

Origen turns the confession into a condition. If we say what Peter said as Peter said it — not by flesh and blood revealing it to us, but by the light from the Father in heaven shining in our heart — then we too become as Peter and are pronounced blessed as he was, because the grounds on which he was pronounced blessed hold equally for us: that flesh and blood did not reveal it, but the Father in heaven, and from the very heavens, so that our citizenship may be in heaven.
17:
Robertson treats the beatitude as an acceptance: the confession is taken as true, and in taking it so the speaker solemnly claims on this occasion to be the Messiah and the Son of the living God, which is to say his deity. He quotes Bruce on the tone — warm, generous, unstinted, not the style of an ecclesiastical editor laying a foundation for church power and prelatic pretensions, but of a noble-minded Master eulogising a loyal disciple. Ellicott, arguing from the reality of that human nature and its capacity for wonder, anger and sorrow, thinks it not over-bold to hear in the words something like a tone of exalted joy; it is the first direct personal beatitude pronounced by him, and stands in marked contrast to the rebukes which had been addressed to the same men as being without understanding, of little faith, their heart yet hardened. Here at last, on his reading, was found the clear and unwavering faith which was the indispensable condition for the manifestation of the kingdom as a visible society upon earth.

Barnes and Clarke both unpack the patronymic, that the name means son of Jona, the first element being the Syriac word for son; and Barnes glosses the blessing itself as happy, honoured, evincing a proper spirit and entitled to the approbation of God.

Lightfoot shows that the phrase about flesh and blood was a Jewish commonplace for opposing men to God, and quotes a run of instances: being led before a king of flesh and blood as against the King of kings; a king of flesh and blood painting his picture on a board as against the Holy Blessed One; and the saying that flesh and blood wound with one thing and heal with another, where the Holy Blessed One wounds and heals with one and the same thing. Clarke insists on that plain sense and complains of the damage done by literalising it, since the words are a Hebrew periphrasis for man, and the literal rendering here and in Galatians has misled thousands into supposing them to mean carnal reason, or the unregenerate principle in man. Wesley glosses them as a man’s own reason or any natural power whatsoever. Barnes alone proposes a different reference, that the words point to the speaker rather than to mankind: this truth you have not learned from my lowly appearance, from my human nature, from my apparent rank and standing in the world.

Calvin asks what the beatitude is for, and widens it. Since eternal life consists in knowing the only true God and him whom he has sent, the man who has honestly made such a confession is justly pronounced happy; and the words were not spoken to Peter in a peculiar manner, the purpose being to show in what the only happiness of the whole world consists. Two things follow for Calvin, and in this order: that all are by nature miserable and accursed until they find a remedy in Christ, so that every man may approach him with the greater courage; and that whoever has obtained Christ wants nothing necessary to perfect happiness, since we have no right to desire anything better.
18:
Robertson locates the stress, following McNeile: not on thou art Peter set against thou art the Christ, but on the and I also — the Father has revealed one truth to you, and I tell you another. The name was prophecy when first given and is now fact. Barnes puts it as a matching of names: in saying that I am the Son of God you called me by a name expressive of my true character, and I have given you one expressive of yours, a rock denoting firmness, which your confession has now shown to be apt. Clarke makes it characteristic of the method, that one whose custom was to rise to heavenly things through earthly takes occasion from the name, whose metaphorical sense was strength and stability, to point out the solidity of the confession and of a cause founded on it.

Lightfoot argues about which language was spoken. Nothing in the dialect of the nation or in reason forbids the thought that the Greek word itself was used, such Graecising being common enough; but granting the more usual assertion that the Syriac word was used, he denies that the very same form occurred twice in the sentence, holding that in the one place it was pronounced after the Greek manner, or in an adjectival form — since otherwise neither the disciples nor Peter could have understood it.

Origen raises the objection that the later controversy turns on, and raises it as a series of questions. If the whole church is built by God on that one man only, what is to be said of John the son of thunder, or of each one of the Apostles? Shall we dare to say that the gates of Hades will not prevail against Peter in particular, but that they will prevail against the other Apostles and the perfect? Does not the promise hold with regard to all of them and in the case of each; and are the keys of the kingdom given to Peter alone? Augustine enters a narrower caution: nobody should suppose Peter received the name here, since he received it where John reports it said to him; and he adds that he has often explained these words as meaning upon him whom Peter had confessed.

Wesley reads the rock as the faith just professed, while allowing another possibility — that the speaker pointed to himself, as he did in saying that this temple should be destroyed, meaning the temple of his body. Wesley is certain at least that Christ is spoken of in Scripture as the only foundation of the Church, that this is what the apostles laid in their preaching, and that it is in respect of laying it that the names of all twelve, and not of one only, were equally inscribed on the twelve foundations of the city of God. Calvin takes the verse as a measure of the pleasure taken in the confession, since so large a reward follows it: the name and the apostleship had already been given out of undeserved goodness, yet those free gifts are here ascribed to faith as though a reward, which Scripture often does. He counts a twofold honour in the sentence, the first part of it relating to Peter’s own advantage.

Cyril of Jerusalem reads the building historically and nationally. After the Jews had been cast away from his grace for the plots they made against the Saviour, a second Holy Church was built out of the Gentiles, the Church of Christians, and it is of that Church that this was said to Peter; Cyril sets the psalmist’s hatred of the congregation of evil-doers against the building of the second. Raban glosses the other half of the promise, taking the gates of hell for the torments and promises by which the enemy attacks, so that what is guaranteed is not immunity from assault but its failure.
19:
Barnes starts from the object itself. A key opens a door, and whoever holds one has power of access and a general charge over a house, which is why Scripture makes it a badge of superintendence and an emblem of authority. He reads this kingdom as Christ’s church on earth, so that what is promised appoints a man to open faith’s door to the world and to preach it first. Robertson sees a building again, unlocked from outside, and asks whether kingdom here means what church meant a verse earlier; he notes that the risen Lord holds death and Hades under lock as well, and that what changes hands belongs properly to a gatekeeper or steward — provided no prerogative peculiar to Peter is read into that office.

Ellicott finds two distinct trains of figurative thought blended in the words. The palace of a great king implied a chief officer, a treasurer or chamberlain, or in the old Hebrew phrase one who was over the household; and the key of office, the key of the gates and of the treasure, was the recognised symbol of it, as in the case of Eliakim the son of Hilkiah. In the highest sense that key of the house of David belonged to Christ himself as the King, who opened and none could shut.

Lightfoot reads the promise as a specific commission: thou shalt first open the door of faith to the Gentiles, which was performed in the story of Cornelius, and he has no doubt that Peter’s words at the council in Jerusalem look back to this sentence. Wesley enters the standing qualification: not to him alone, since the keys were equally given to all the apostles at the same time, but to him they were given first, both of doctrine and of discipline — he first exercised the apostleship after the resurrection and first by preaching opened the kingdom to Jews and then to Gentiles; and under binding and loosing are contained all the acts of discipline which he and his brethren performed as apostles.

Clarke adds a rabbinic parallel. He understands this kingdom as Christ’s true Church, and the keys as power to admit into that house or keep an unfit person out — which amounts to a doctrine of salvation and a full declaration of how God saves sinners; and he recalls that a Jewish doctor of the law was invested by having put into his hand a key to the temple closet where sacred books lay, together with tablets to write on. Calvin treats the sentence as introducing a new subject, public office, which he dignifies twice over: ministers are porters, so to speak, carrying what unlocks heaven, and they wield a power ratified above. He thinks the figure belongs properly to teaching, since Luke charges scribes and Pharisees with holding those same keys. Origen binds this gift to the preceding promise, for whoever stands fortified so that Hades cannot prevail against him is the man fit to receive from that same Word what unlocks heaven, and he receives it as a prize.
20:
Barnes reports the force of the verb: Mark and Luke have him strictly or severely charging them, laying emphasis on it as a matter of much importance; and the reason he gives is that the time had not fully come, and that the speaker was unwilling to rouse Jewish malice and endanger his life by having the thing proclaimed. Clarke supplies the textual detail behind that: some very good manuscripts use a word meaning that he threatened them, the reading of the Codex Bezae in both Greek and Latin, and the name Jesus is omitted by fifty-four manuscripts, some of the greatest authority and antiquity, as well as by the Syriac, the later Persic and Arabic, the Slavonic, six copies of the Itala and several fathers, so that Griesbach left it out of the text. Barnes agrees the word should probably be dropped.

On the motive the three agree and differ only in emphasis. Robertson gives it shortly: for the very reason that he had avoided the claim in public, since he was the Messiah but the people would inevitably take the word in a political sense; he thinks the speaker was profoundly moved by the confession and confident of the final outcome, yet foresaw peril to them all. Ellicott analyses the reticence further. Had the disciples gone about sounding the watchword that the Christ had come, it would not have been difficult to gather round him the homage of excited crowds; but it was not that homage he sought, and such preaching tended to present a false aspect of the kingdom and to prevent the consummation he was now directing them towards. Wesley notes that he had not said it expressly even to the apostles but left them to infer it from his doctrine and miracles, and that it was not proper for them to say it openly before the grand proof of it, his resurrection — since those who believed them would the more earnestly have sought to take him and make him a king, and those who did not would the more vehemently have rejected such a Messiah.

Jerome notices an apparent contradiction with the earlier commission to preach his advent, and resolves it by a distinction: it is one thing to preach Christ and another to preach Jesus the Christ, the first being a common title of dignity and the second the proper name of the Saviour. Origen offers two accounts instead. Either they had spoken of him until now in lowly words, as a great and wonderful man, without yet proclaiming him as the Christ; or, if he had been proclaimed as Christ from the first, then what he now chose was that the short early announcement of the name should be left in silence and not repeated. Chrysostom explains why the sorrowful things are dwelt on in its place: what has once taken root and then been torn up is retained with difficulty among the multitude if it is planted a second time, where what was once rooted and has continued unmoved is easily brought on to further growth.
21:
Ellicott takes the prominence given to the prediction as evidence that it struck the disciples as something altogether new. They had failed to understand the mysterious hints already given — the destroying of the temple, the Son of Man being lifted up, the sign of the prophet Jonah — and now the veil is lifted and the order of events plainly foretold: the entry into Jerusalem, the rejection, the condemnation, the death, the resurrection. He adds that if the record is accepted as true the prediction implies a foreknowledge which is at least supernatural. Robertson dates the disclosure, a little over six months before the cross, and calls the moment suitable: they had to know it now in order to be ready then, and the great confession made the occasion appropriate; the warnings now begun would be repeated twice more, with the betrayal named at one and the cross at the other.

Why it was not said sooner is answered the same way by four of them. Barnes observes that this is the first intimation of a death in that cruel manner: much pains had been taken to convince them that he was the Messiah, the confession showed they were convinced, and only then did the preparing of their minds begin — had the thing been declared when they were first called they would never have followed, since they were expecting a temporal and triumphant prince. Clarke says that before this he had spoken of his death only vaguely and obscurely, because he would not afflict his disciples sooner than necessity required, and that now, with the time drawing near, he spoke in the most express and clear terms. Henry gives the same reason, that the disciples were weak and could not well bear the notice of a thing so strange and so melancholy. Gill adds two of his own: their faith was by now well grounded and established, so that they could bear what would earlier have staggered them, and being forewarned they would be forearmed.

Clarke counts three sorts of persons named as the cause of the passion, the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and passes on Quesnel’s observation that Christ is generally persecuted by those three descriptions of men. Wesley names them with the same irony: the elders were the most honourable and experienced men, the chief priests were accounted the most religious, and the scribes were the most learned body in the nation, and one would have expected these to be the very first to receive him. Wesley also marks the change in the teaching itself — hitherto they had mainly been taught one point, that he was the Christ, and from this time another, that Christ must enter his glory through sufferings and death.

Origen draws out what the confession changed for the preachers. Whoever holds that the charge given to the Twelve belongs to a later time, and that the Apostles had not yet announced him as the Christ, will say that the conception of the Christ wrapped up in the name of Jesus was being reserved for a more perfect preaching, the preaching which brought salvation — the kind Paul knew of when he determined to know nothing among the Corinthians save Jesus Christ and him crucified. On that reading they had formerly proclaimed Jesus as the doer of certain things and the teacher of certain things, and what is new from this point is not the person but what there is to say about him.
22:
Robertson reads the gesture out of the middle voice: taking him to himself, aside and apart, as if by a right of his own. He quotes Bengel, that the man acted with greater familiarity once the token of acknowledgment had been given and was promptly reduced to his level again, and Bruce, that Peter appears here in a new character, speaking a minute ago under inspiration from heaven and now under inspiration from the opposite quarter. Clarke renders the verb as taking him up, interrupting him suddenly as though calling him to order, and notes that other versions give it the sense of calling aside, while the word can also mean to receive in a friendly manner. Barnes prefers that friendlier sense, a hand laid on him as a friend’s, and reads the exclamation as an abbreviated prayer, that God would be merciful to him. Gill collects the versions, where the Arabic has called to him, the Ethiopic answered him, the Syriac led him and the Persic privately said to him.

Ellicott explains the remonstrance from where the hearer’s attention stopped. His mind dwelt on the former and not the latter part of the prediction: the death was plain and terrible to him because he failed to grasp the idea of the resurrection. The protest might have been natural at any time, but the contrast between this prediction and the confidence of the promise just given intensified its vehemence; personal love for his Lord and his own desire to share in the glory that promise implied were united in the refusal.

Jerome measures the fault generously. Peter had too hot a zeal and a very great affection towards the Saviour, and after that confession and the reward he had just heard he would not have his confession destroyed, thinking it impossible that the Son of God should be put to death; so he takes him aside rather than seem to rebuke his Master before his fellow disciples, and chides him with the feeling of a man who loved him. Hilary refuses to let the harder word fall on Peter at all: the order to get behind is an order to follow the example of the passion, while the naming of Satan and of an offence is turned on the one who suggested the thought, since we cannot suppose such a name imputed to Peter after so great declarations of blessedness. Chrysostom asks what wonder it is that this should befall a man who had received no revelation about these things, and makes the lapse evidence for the confession: in matters not revealed to him he is plainly at a loss, estimating the things of Christ by human and earthly principles and so judging suffering mean and unworthy of him.

Origen puts the fault theologically: while the beginnings of these things were still being spoken, Peter judged them unworthy of the Son of the living God, forgetting that the Son of the living God does nothing worthy of blame, and so began to rebuke him as though Christ himself had needed a propitiation; his affection is allowed and his ignorance charged. Calvin is the sharpest of them. The zeal is excessive, though the respect appears in his not venturing to reprove his Master in front of others; and it was highly presumptuous all the same to advise our Lord as if he had been deficient in prudence or self-command, since men hurried on by inconsiderate zeal do not hesitate to pass judgment on God himself according to their own fancy.
23:
Robertson reads the turn as a movement of revulsion, a quick ingressive aorist away from Peter and towards the other disciples. A moment before, he says, Peter had played the part of a rock in the noble confession and been given a place of leadership; now he is playing the part of Satan and is ordered to the rear, tempting his Master not to go on to the cross as the wilderness tempter had done — and he adds the warning that none are more formidable instruments of temptation than well-meaning friends who care more for our comfort than for our character. Gill notes that the argument had been private and the reproof was not: what was said was so offensive that the rebuke was given publicly, before the disciples. Ellicott takes the same point from Mark, who adds that he turned about and looked on them; they stood behind, watching the effect of a remonstrance their spokesman had made for them, and the rebuke, though addressed to him, was spoken so that they should hear it too.

Whether the word is as harsh as it looks divides them squarely. Barnes and Clarke both soften it by translation. The word means literally an adversary, one who opposes us in the accomplishment of our designs, and though it is commonly applied to the devil there is no evidence of its being applied to Peter in that sense, or used in anger: the meaning may be that such sentiments as he had expressed were opposed to Christ and his plans. Clarke renders it get behind me, thou adversary, says this is the proper translation and that it takes away the harshness which the usual rendering carries, and glosses the next clause as thou art a stumbling-block in my way. Ellicott and Wesley go the other way. Ellicott finds in the sharpness a strong and intense emotion, the chief of the Apostles addressed in the self-same terms as the Tempter, because this was nothing less than a renewal of the same temptation. Wesley observes that no other apostle is recorded to have received so sharp a reproof on any occasion, thinks it needful for the pride of a heart puffed up with the commendation lately given, and takes the word to mean not merely that he was an enemy while fancying himself the best of friends, but that he was acting the very part of Satan.

Calvin dismisses one line of speculation about the preposition, that Peter was being ordered to follow and not to go before; the same words were used in repelling the wilderness attack, and the Greek simply means to withdraw and be gone, so that the disciple is thrown to a distance for having acted the adversary’s part. Origen builds on the comparison Calvin rejects. Set beside what was said to the devil, this saying adds the words behind me, which the other did not; and being behind Jesus is a good thing, as the call to come behind him and be made fishers of men shows, and the saying about taking up a cross and following behind him.
24:
Chrysostom supplies the join. The rebuke alone did not satisfy, and over and above it the impropriety of what Peter had said and the fruit of the passion had to be shown. Your word to me is that this shall not be, Chrysostom paraphrases, and my word to you is that hindering me is not merely hurtful: it will be impossible for you to be saved unless you too are crucified. Gill explains who needed to hear it: they had all imbibed the same notion of a temporal kingdom and expected worldly riches, honour and pleasure, so the doctrine of the cross was preached to them now, with a warning to prepare for persecution and death. Ellicott notes from Mark that the multitude was called along with the disciples, and from Luke’s wording that the same is implied: the teaching about the unworldliness of the kingdom is generalised as widely as possible, so that men following in idle wonder or from a desire of earthly greatness should know the conditions. Calvin says the same: seeing that Peter dreaded the cross and the rest were affected in the same way, Christ enters on a general discourse and lays down one law for all the godly rather than for the twelve alone.

Two small grammatical points carry weight here. Ellicott insists that the will is more than an auxiliary — whoever willeth, desireth to come after. Robertson contrasts the tenses of the two commands, an aorist for picking up the cross at once and a present for the following, which is to be kept up; and he adds that cross-bearing was a familiar figure to men who knew the crucifixion of criminals at Jerusalem. The saying is pertinent just here because Christ’s own cross faces him and Peter had dared to pull him away from it.

Gregory presses the paradox in denying oneself. Unless a man departs from himself he does not draw near to him who is above him; but if we leave ourselves, where are we to go, and who is it that goes? His answer is that we are one thing when fallen by sin and another as we were made by nature, so that we deny ourselves when we avoid what we were of old and strive towards what we are called to in newness — whoever is changed for the better begins to be what he was not and ceases to be what he was. Barnes puts it as a surrender to God of will, affections, body and soul, with a man’s own happiness given up as the supreme object. Wesley makes it a daily rule, that a man deny his own will however pleasing and do God’s however painful, and asks whether all crosses should not be reckoned opportunities of embracing God’s will at the expense of our own. Clarke numbers three principles: a sincere desire to belong to Christ, the renouncing of self-dependence, and the embracing of whatever condition God appoints.

Origen makes belief in the cross the test rather than mere abstinence from sin: a man may seem to keep clear of sin and still not be crucified with Christ if he does not believe in that cross. He then states the exchange both ways. Whoever loves this life and spares it, fearing to die and supposing that life ends at this death, loses it by estranging it from life eternal; whoever despises it and contends for truth to the point of death loses it only so far as this life goes. Hilary allows a lesser form of the same thing, that we follow by taking up the cross of his passion, and if not in deed then in will bear him company. Jerome turns it into a single sentence: he takes up his cross who is crucified to the world, and the man to whom the world is crucified follows his crucified Lord.
25:
Robertson calls it a paradoxical play on one word, used in two senses, and the same with the saving and the losing. Ellicott finds a subtler distinction which the English fails to carry: the first clause has whoever willeth, wishes, to save his life, where the second has simply whoever shall lose it — as though it were felt that no man could wish to lose his life for the sake of losing it, however ready he might be to surrender it if called on. He adds that the word rendered life here is the same word rendered soul in the next verse.

Gill describes the man meant in detail: one desirous of preserving himself from troubles, reproaches, persecutions and death, who takes the method of forsaking Christ, denying his Gospel and dropping his profession of it, and so currying favour with men in order to secure worldly emoluments, honour, peace, pleasure and life. Clarke adds the irony of the outcome, that a man who wishes to save his life at the expense of his conscience, casting the cross aside, meets the very evil he wished to avoid and loses his soul into the bargain, while whatever a man loses here for a steady attachment to Christ is amply made up to him in the eternal world. Wesley sets the test at its highest: whoever will not renounce himself in the one instance of life itself shall be lost eternally — and he asks how a man can hope to manage that renunciation if he cannot manage it in the smallest instances.

Origen notes that the first expression is ambiguous, and takes it this way: if anyone, being a lover of life and thinking the present life good, tends his own life carefully with a view to living in the flesh, afraid to die because he supposes death will lose it for him, then by the very willing to save it so he loses it, placing it outside the borders of blessedness. Calvin reads the second clause as a most appropriate consolation, that men who willingly suffer death for Christ’s sake actually obtain life, a motive Mark states expressly and which must be understood here. He enters one caution: irreligious men are frequently prompted by ambition or despair to despise life, and it will be no advantage to such persons that they met death courageously. The threatening set against the promise he thinks powerfully calculated to shake off carnal sloth.
26:
Chrysostom explains why a question about profit should follow a paradox about losing. Saving had been set against losing, and lest anyone conclude that the two were of equal weight, the question is added: do not say that the man who escapes the dangers threatening him for Christ’s sake has saved his soul, meaning his temporal life — add the whole world to that temporal life, and what will any of it profit him if his soul perishes for ever?

Clarke protests at the English rendering. On what authority many have translated the same word as life in the previous verse and soul in this one he does not know, and he is certain it means life in both: if a man gained the whole world, its riches, honours and pleasures, and lost his life, what would any of it profit him, seeing it can only be enjoyed during life? Yet he grants that if the words be applied to the soul they show the difficulty, the necessity and the importance of salvation. Ellicott agrees that the English introduces an apparent antithesis of language in place of the identity of the original, and would keep life in both places. Barnes keeps the stronger sense and spells it out: gaining the whole world means possessing it as our own, with all its riches, honours and pleasures, and losing the soul means being cast away and shut out of heaven. He finds two things implied, that men striving after the world and unwilling to give it up for religion will lose their souls, and that once the soul is lost nothing can be given in exchange for it.

On the exchange itself the three converge from different directions. Robertson notes that both verbs are aorist subjunctives and so punctiliar, a supposed case, and that the verb for forfeiting occurs in the papyri of being fined or mulcted of money; the soul has no market price, whatever the devil may think, and a man must surrender his life and nothing less, no exchange being possible. Origen considers the obvious candidate and rejects it: at first sight the ransom might be supposed to lie in a man’s substance, that he should give it to the poor and so save his soul, but Origen holds that a man has nothing which, offered as a ransom for his soul, would deliver it from death — God gave that ransom himself. Calvin says the word is used here in the strictest sense, and reads the question as a reminder that man was not created merely to enjoy the world for a few days but to obtain immortality in heaven at last; what carelessness and brutal stupidity it is, he asks, that men should be so attached to the world as never to consider why they were born.

Ellicott defends the form of the argument, which might look unworthy. It is not without purpose that what may be called the argument of expediency is brought in here, since even the self-denial just required does not exclude the thought, for men still within reach of such reasoning, of what will profit them most in the long run; and there is a self-love which, for all the strained language of an exaggerated and unreal philanthropy, is ennobling rather than debasing. Gregory distinguishes two periods instead, and matches the commands to them: the Church has a time of persecution and a time of peace, and where in persecution the life itself is to be laid down, in peace it is those earthly lusts which might gain too great a power over us that have to be broken through.
27:
Ellicott makes the verse an argument rather than an appendix: the coming of the Son of Man to execute judgment clothes the abstract statement just made with an awful certainty, since no bribe can be offered to the Eternal Judge to alter a sentence of forfeiture rightfully incurred. He notes besides that this claim to be the future Judge of all men is never absent from our Lord’s teaching from first to last, asserted in every great discourse and implied in almost every parable. Wesley compresses the whole into a line, that there is no way to escape the righteous judgment of God. Barnes fills in the scene: he will come in the glory of his Father, the majesty with which God is accustomed to appear, attended by angels and judging all men, rewarding the righteous in heaven and sending the wicked away as a recompense for their works.

Clarke refers the sentence elsewhere, to Daniel’s vision of one like the Son of Man coming to the Ancient of Days and receiving dominion and glory and a kingdom which all peoples should serve. On that reading what is meant is the mediatorial kingdom Christ was then about to set up, by the destruction of the Jewish nation and polity and the spreading of his Gospel through the whole world; and if the words are taken so, the angels or messengers may signify the apostles and their successors. Gill treats the verse as the proof of what precedes, establishing that lives may be lost by saving them and found by losing them, and pointing out the time when all this will appear.

Origen sets the two comings against each other. He has not yet come in his glory, for we saw him and he had no form nor beauty, his form dishonoured and defective compared with the sons of men, a man in affliction and toil and acquainted with the enduring of sickness; and it was necessary that he should come in such a form if he was to bear our sins and suffer pain for us, since bearing our sins did not become him in glory. Calvin explains why the judgment is produced just here. The doctrine laid down has to affect our minds more deeply, and we cannot perceive the worthlessness of this fading life unless we are deeply affected by the view of the heavenly one — so tardy and sluggish is the mind that it needs the help of looking towards heaven. Believers are summoned to the judgment-seat so that they may reflect at all times that they lived for no other object than to long after that blessed redemption.
28:
Robertson lists the candidates and refuses to choose: the Transfiguration, the Resurrection, Pentecost, the destruction of Jerusalem, the Second Coming and Judgment. We do not know, he says, only that Jesus was certain of a final victory which would be typified and symbolised in various ways; and the apocalyptic symbolism used here does not dominate the teaching, being employed at times to picture the kingdom’s triumph rather than to set out the whole doctrine of it. Origen reports the commonest answer, that the words look six days ahead — eight, as Luke counts — to the going up of the three into the high mountain, so that those three did not taste death before they saw the Son of Man coming in his own kingdom, since in seeing a face that shone they saw the kingdom of God coming with power. Chrysostom supplies the motive for giving any such proof: having discoursed much of dangers and death, of his own passion and the slaughter of his disciples, and having laid severe injunctions on them, he had put the hardships in the present and at hand while the good things remained in hope, and so was willing to assure their very sight of what kind of glory he would come with, so far as they could learn it.

Ellicott dissents from the Transfiguration reading, with a reason drawn from the wording. The immediate sequence of that vision has led not a few interpreters to find the fulfilment there, but a closer scrutiny of the words sets the interpretation aside, except so far as the Transfiguration bore witness to what had till then been the latent possibilities of his greatness: something due to happen within six days is not naturally described as what some standing there should not taste death before seeing. Barnes rules out the other extreme, that it cannot refer to the end of the world, and sees no need to refer it to the destruction of Jerusalem either, noting that Mark and Luke explain the phrase — the one having it that they should see the kingdom of God come with power. Clarke takes the Jerusalem reading outright: the words speak of the Church established after Pentecost and triumphant after the destruction of the Jewish polity, which fell some forty-three years later, when several of those present doubtless survived to see the kingdom extended. Wesley agrees, that some there should live to see the mediatorial kingdom set up with great power by the increase of the Church and the destruction of the temple, city and polity of the Jews.

Calvin reads the promise as an interim concession. The disciples might still hesitate and ask when that day would be, and they are animated by the assurance that a proof of the future glory would presently be given; for to a man in expectation even speed looks like delay, and never more so than when we are told to wait for our salvation until the coming of Christ. So an intermediate period is held out for confirmation, as much as to say that if the day of his coming seems too long to wait for, he will provide against the waiting. Gill marks the strength of the asseveration, that Christ puts his own Amen to it and declares a certain truth which may firmly be believed. Raban glosses the tasting of death, that it is said of the saints, by whom the death of the body is tasted as though sipped, while the life of the soul is held fast in possession. Remigius applies the fulfilment to the three who went up, to whom the Lord transfigured showed the joys of the eternal inheritance and who saw him coming in his kingdom, which is to say shining in that radiance in which all the saints shall behold him after the judgment is passed.
